headline: San Francisco approves first gay bathhouse since AIDS epidemic
author: N. Kirkpatrick

paragraphs.text: San Francisco, the crusading city for gay rights and sexual liberation, closed its last legal bathhouses during the ravages of the AIDS epidemic.
Now, for the first time in nearly 40 years, the city has authorized a new gay bathhouse.

The San Francisco Planning Commission approved permits last week for Sanctum Baths. The plans call for the conversion of a two-story, 7,516-square-foot commercial building into a bathhouse and “adult sex venue” in The Hub neighborhood, next to the historic Leather & LGBTQ Cultural District. Backers of the project, first reported by the Bay Area Reporter, expect it to open by the end of next year.
Sanctum is first adult bath to be approved since the San Francisco Board of Supervisors rescinded its AIDS-era ban on them in 2020, according to the San Francisco Chronicle.

San Francisco had as many as 20 baths at their peak in 1982, according to Jacob Binder writing in the Berkeley Journal of Gender, Law & Justice. The spaces, which typically included saunas and steam rooms, served as gathering spaces and safe havens for sexual contact without harassment by law enforcement. In the 1970s, they became political symbols for the gay liberation movement.

“The baths were hallowed sites of queer community-building and epicenters of the city’s sexual subcultures,” Binder wrote. At first the bathhouses had few regulations or legal restrictions and hosted as many as 12,000 patrons a month. But the AIDS epidemic devastated the lives of gay men and became a new catalyst of prejudice against them. A “mix of caution, declining business, and government persecution” closed all the bathhouses by 1987.

Now, as new drugs for the treatment of HIV and AIDS have vastly reduced the transmission of the virus and the lethality of the disease, other cities such as Minneapolis and San Diego have rolled back AIDS-era policies.
“For decades sex positive spaces were systematically stigmatized and forced out of existence,” Jonathan Ohene, a local business owner and cultural district board member said in public comment.
”Approving this project is a vital step towards healing that painful chapter of our history," he said. “It’s exactly what our neighborhood needs.”
